newsitem.title: USA: Uganda warned against diverting debt money to arms.
newsitem.headline: Uganda warned against diverting debt money to arms.

text.p: The World Bank has warned Uganda, the first to benefit from a debt relief plan for poor nations, it must not divert money from this into military spending, World Bank head James Wolfensohn said on Friday.

"I have personally discussed this with Ugandan President (Yoweri) Museveni. We have had assurances from the Ugandans that they are not using this money for military expenditure," Wolfensohn told a news conference.

"We are going to watch it very carefully. We have made our position very clear with President Museveni and the Ugandans. We have told them if the value of military expenditure becomes a major issue, we will have major problems," he added.

Earlier this week the World Bank and International Monetary Fund approved debt relief for Uganda which will reduce its debt by about a fifth, freeing up funds for use in schools, hospitals and other social programmes.
Wolfensohn said Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Bolivia would be next to benefit, with debt relief packages for these three countries likely to be approved in the coming months.

The initiative, to be carried out jointly with the Paris Club of creditor nations, is meant to lift poor countries, mostly in Africa, out of a debt trap where debt repayments wipe out all the benefits of economic growth.

But it has run into controversy in Africa, caught up in competition by rich nations for influence in the continent and by fall-out from the civil war in Zaire, where many countries, including Uganda, are alleged to be helping rebels.
Diplomats had said earlier that worries about a rise in Ugandan military spending had been a big sticking point in talks on giving it debt relief.
France in the meantime fought hard to ensure Ivory Coast, a former colony and key ally in west Africa, would also benefit from the debt initiative, alongside former British colony Uganda.

Aid agencies have slammed the debt relief programme as insufficient. Aid agency Oxfam said on Thursday "high-level horse-trading" between rich nations was leading to longer than justified delays in helping poor countries.
Wolfensohn lashed out at criticism, saying for the first time in history the World Bank had reduced debt.
"I was hoping in my dreams that when all this happened I would get a standing ovation. Instead of which people say you are a son-of-a-bitch," he said.

He said he expected the World Bank and IMF to agree shortly to widening the criteria on which countries qualify for debt relief to take account of government revenues as well as export revenues. This would allow Ivory Coast to benefit from the initiative.
But though France had argued for a widening of the criteria, Wolfensohn said the decision would be made as one of principle "and not related to pressure from any country".
"It will not be because of France or anyone," he said.
Wolfensohn also called for peace in Zaire, saying its civil war was hindering economic development.
"You cannot have that level of conflict and not have a significant impact on economic development. You have to have peace before you can have economic development," he said.
Forces led by rebel leader Laurent Kabila fighting to oust Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko have overrun more than half of Zaire.
